definition: deeply religious; or pretending to be morally good

examples.text: The pious queen founded a monastery in every province she visited.
The landlord's pious speeches about charity do not stop him from raising the rent.
My grandmother is pious and has not missed a Sunday service in forty years.

confused.note: Pious means devout; piteous means deserving pity.

questions.passage: The merchant was known throughout the town as a ______ man. He prayed at dawn and dusk, gave a tenth of his income to the temple, and would not open his shop on any holy day.
questions.explanation: Daily prayer, temple gifts, and keeping holy days show deep religious devotion.

distractors.why: Frivolous means not serious, the opposite of such devoted habits.
Affluent means wealthy; the details given are about devotion, not riches.
Contentious means quarrelsome, which is not described.

definition: a perfect example of a quality or type

examples.text: With her quiet courage, the nurse is the epitome of the novel's ideal of duty.
The palace was the epitome of royal extravagance.
My grandfather, in his pressed shirt and polished shoes, is the epitome of neatness.

confused.note: An epitome is a perfect example; an epitaph is an inscription on a tomb.

questions.passage: Calm under pressure, generous in victory, and gracious in defeat, the team's captain was the ______ of good sportsmanship, and younger players were told to watch how she behaved.
questions.explanation: Someone held up as the model for others is a perfect example.

distractors.why: Antithesis means the direct opposite, which she was not.
A paradigm is a model or pattern of thinking in a field; a person who shows a quality perfectly is its epitome.
A plethora is an excess, which does not fit.

definition: needing or using a lot of effort and energy

examples.text: Strenuous exercise raises the heart rate for hours afterward.
Despite strenuous objections from the admirals, the fleet sailed in winter.
Moving the couch up the stairs was more strenuous than any gym workout.

confused.note: Strenuous means requiring effort; strident means loud and harsh.

questions.passage: Doctors told the recovering patient that gentle walks were fine but that he should avoid anything ______. Lifting heavy boxes, running, and climbing long flights of stairs would have to wait another month.
questions.explanation: Lifting, running, and long climbs demand great effort.

distractors.why: Sedentary means involving sitting, which is not what the doctors forbade.
Frivolous means silly or unimportant, which is not the distinction the doctors draw.
Oblique means indirect or slanting, which does not fit.

definition: impossible to satisfy

examples.text: The dragon's insatiable greed empties every treasury in the kingdom.
The growing city had an insatiable demand for timber.
My little cousin has an insatiable curiosity and asks "why" about everything.

confused.note: Insatiable means never satisfied; insensible means unconscious or unaware.

questions.passage: The young naturalist had an ______ appetite for facts about insects. Having read every book in the school library on the subject, she began writing to university professors to ask what else there was to learn.
questions.explanation: Exhausting a library and still wanting more shows a desire that cannot be satisfied.

distractors.why: Precarious means dangerously unstable, which does not describe an appetite for knowledge.
Stagnant means not moving or growing, the opposite of her eager pursuit.
Frivolous means not serious, but her interest was intense.

partsNote: from Latin satis, "enough": not able to get enough

definition: to give up a position of power or fail to carry out a duty

examples.text: The king abdicated in 1936, and his brother took the throne.
The father abdicates all responsibility and leaves his children to the governess.
I refuse to abdicate my role as official pancake flipper.

confused.note: To abdicate is to give up a position; to abrogate is to cancel a law or agreement.

questions.passage: Faced with riots in the capital and an army that would no longer obey him, the emperor chose to ______. He signed a brief statement renouncing the crown and left the country that night.
questions.explanation: Renouncing the crown is giving up a position of power.

distractors.why: Appease means to calm by giving in, and it needs an object; it does not mean giving up a throne.
Endorse means to approve publicly, which does not fit.
Agitate means to stir up, the opposite of withdrawing.

definition: to make someone upset or nervous; or to argue publicly for change

examples.text: Workers agitated for a ten-hour day throughout the 1840s.
The machine agitates the mixture until the powder dissolves.
Loud thunder always agitates our dog.

confused.note: To agitate is to stir up or upset; to aggravate is to make worse.

questions.passage: The zookeeper asked visitors not to tap on the glass. The noise, she explained, would ______ the snakes, which might then strike at the pane and injure themselves.
questions.explanation: Tapping upsets the snakes and makes them strike.

distractors.why: Appease means to calm or pacify, the opposite of what tapping does.
Endorse means to approve, which does not fit.
Abdicate means to give up power, which does not fit.

definition: a natural tendency to do or like something, often something bad

examples.text: The hero's proclivity for gambling costs him the family estate.
Some breeds show a proclivity for herding even without training.
I have a proclivity for leaving essays until the night before.

confused.note: A proclivity is a tendency; proximity is nearness.

questions.passage: Editors learned to check the columnist's figures carefully. He had a ______ for exaggeration, routinely turning "several" into "dozens" and "a slight rise" into "a dramatic surge."
questions.explanation: Routinely inflating numbers is a habitual tendency.

distractors.why: An aversion is a strong dislike, the opposite of a habit he indulged.
A zenith is a highest point, which does not fit.
A conundrum is a difficult problem, which does not describe a habit.

definition: extremely important and urgent

examples.text: It is imperative that the samples stay frozen during transport.
The general thought it imperative to cross the river before the rains.
It is imperative that you call Grandma back today; she has called four times.

confused.note: Imperative means urgent and necessary; imperious means arrogantly commanding.

questions.passage: With the reservoir at a tenth of its capacity and no rain forecast, officials declared it ______ that residents reduce their water use at once. Those who ignored the order would face fines.
questions.explanation: A nearly empty reservoir makes cutting water use urgently necessary.

distractors.why: Frivolous means unimportant, the opposite of an urgent order.
Oblique means indirect, which does not describe an urgent need.
Archaic means very old-fashioned, which does not fit.

definition: able to do many different things or be used in many ways

examples.text: Carbon is a versatile element that forms millions of compounds.
The versatile general was also a poet, an engineer, and a fine cook.
A versatile jacket works for school, a hike, and a rainy bus stop.

confused.note: Versatile means able to do many things; volatile means unstable.

questions.passage: Critics praised the actor as unusually ______. In a single season she played a grieving queen, a fast-talking salesman, and a silent clown, and was equally convincing in each role.
questions.explanation: Playing very different roles equally well shows wide-ranging ability.

distractors.why: Stagnant means not developing, the opposite of such range.
Contentious means quarrelsome, which is not what critics praised.
Precarious means insecure, which does not fit.

definition: to say publicly that you support or approve of someone or something

examples.text: Three former governors endorsed the young candidate.
The medical association endorsed the new screening guidelines.
My coach endorsed my plan to try out for goalie.

confused.note: Endorse means to support publicly; endure means to last or to suffer patiently.

questions.passage: The newspaper had never before taken sides in a mayoral race. This year, however, its editors decided to ______ a candidate, explaining in a front-page editorial why they believed she deserved readers' votes.
questions.explanation: Explaining why a candidate deserves votes is publicly supporting her.

distractors.why: Censure means to criticize formally, the opposite of supporting.
Appease means to pacify by giving in, which is not what the editors did.
Abdicate means to give up power, which does not fit.

partsNote: from Latin dorsum, "back": to write on the back

definition: a natural liking for or connection with someone or something

examples.text: The molecule has a strong affinity for oxygen and binds to it readily.
The two outsiders feel an immediate affinity for each other.
I have always had an affinity for rainy days and long books.

confused.note: Affinity is a natural liking or closeness; infinity is endlessness.

questions.passage: Though raised in a desert town, the painter felt a lifelong ______ for the sea. She moved to the coast at eighteen and spent the next fifty years painting almost nothing but waves and harbors.
questions.explanation: Being drawn to the sea all her life is a natural liking.

distractors.why: Antipathy is strong dislike, the opposite of her attraction.
A paradigm is a model or pattern, which does not fit.
A plethora is an excess, which does not fit "for the sea."

definition: a typical example or model; a widely accepted way of thinking about something

examples.text: Plate tectonics replaced the old paradigm of fixed continents.
The factory became the paradigm for how work was organized in the new century.
Our teacher wants to shift the paradigm from memorizing facts to asking questions.

confused.note: A paradigm is a model or framework; a paradox is a seeming contradiction.

questions.passage: For two centuries Newton's laws supplied the ______ within which physicists worked. Einstein's theories did not merely add to that framework; they replaced it with a new way of understanding space and time.
questions.explanation: A framework within which a whole field works is a paradigm.

distractors.why: A paradox is a seeming contradiction; it resembles the right word but means something else.
A zenith is a highest point, not a framework.
An affinity is a natural liking, which does not fit.

partsNote: from Greek deiknynai, "to show": to show side by side

definition: relating to the brain; or appealing to the intellect more than to the emotions

examples.text: The scan revealed reduced blood flow in the cerebral cortex.
Critics found the novel too cerebral, all ideas and no heart.
Chess is a cerebral game, which is why I prefer dodgeball.

confused.note: Cerebral relates to the brain or intellect; celestial relates to the sky or heavens.

questions.passage: Audiences who want car chases should look elsewhere. The film is a ______ thriller whose tension comes entirely from two detectives reasoning their way, clue by clue, toward a conclusion.
questions.explanation: Tension that comes from reasoning appeals to the intellect.

distractors.why: Frivolous means silly and unserious, which this thoughtful film is not.
Archaic means very old-fashioned, which is not the contrast with car chases.
Affluent means wealthy, which does not describe a film.

definition: to give official approval for something; or, as a noun, an official penalty

examples.text: The council sanctioned the building of a new harbor wall.
The ethics board refused to sanction the experiment.
The school does not sanction skipping class, even for a championship parade.

confused.note: To sanction is to approve officially; a sanctuary is a safe place.

questions.passage: The league had long tolerated the practice without comment. Last year it went further and formally ______ it, adding a rule that explicitly permits coaches to speak with players during play.
questions.explanation: Adding a rule that permits the practice is official approval.

distractors.why: Proscribed means forbade, the opposite of adding a rule that permits.
Agitated means stirred up, which does not fit.
Abdicated means gave up power, which does not fit.

definition: having a lot of money and a high standard of living

examples.text: Affluent merchants built the tall brick houses along the canal.
Studies show that affluent neighborhoods have more street trees.
The school draws students from both affluent suburbs and working farms.

confused.note: Affluent means wealthy; effluent is liquid waste flowing out.

questions.passage: The district is one of the most ______ in the country. Its median household income is three times the national figure, and its public schools have swimming pools and theaters.
questions.explanation: High incomes and lavish schools indicate wealth.

distractors.why: Destitute means extremely poor, the opposite of this district.
Pious means devout, which the passage does not discuss.
Stagnant means not growing, which is not the point.

definition: very old and no longer in ordinary use

examples.text: The poem's archaic spellings, such as "olde" and "shoppe," are deliberate.
The archaic law required every citizen to own a longbow.
My grandfather's archaic phone has a dial and a cord.

confused.note: Archaic means very old or old-fashioned; arcane means known to only a few.

questions.passage: The court's procedures strike visitors as ______. Lawyers still address the judge in phrases from the 1600s, and documents must be submitted on paper of a size that no ordinary printer has used for a century.
questions.explanation: Phrases from the 1600s and outdated paper sizes are very old-fashioned.

distractors.why: Versatile means adaptable, which these rigid procedures are not.
Imperative means urgent, which does not describe old customs.
Precarious means unstable, which does not fit.

definition: causing or likely to cause disagreement; fond of arguing

examples.text: The contentious question of who would pay for the war split the cabinet.
The contentious uncle turns every family dinner into a debate.
Where to put the new stop sign became a surprisingly contentious issue on our street.

confused.note: Contentious means causing argument; content means satisfied.

questions.passage: The proposal to rename the town's main street proved highly ______. Public meetings on the subject ran past midnight, neighbors stopped speaking to one another, and the council received more letters than on any issue in its history.
questions.explanation: Long meetings, feuding neighbors, and floods of letters show the proposal caused disagreement.

distractors.why: Frivolous means unimportant, but residents clearly cared a great deal.
Pious means devout, which does not fit.
Oblique means indirect, which does not describe a hotly debated proposal.

definition: not flowing or moving; not growing or developing

examples.text: Mosquitoes breed in stagnant water left in old tires and buckets.
Wages remained stagnant for a decade while prices rose.
The pond grew stagnant and green after the pump broke.

confused.note: Stagnant means not moving or growing; staunch means firmly loyal.

questions.passage: While its rivals introduced new models every year, the company's product line remained ______. The catalog it mailed in 2010 was almost identical to the one it had mailed in 1995.
questions.explanation: A catalog unchanged for fifteen years shows no development.

distractors.why: Versatile means adaptable and varied, the opposite of an unchanging product line.
Precarious means insecure; the passage describes a lack of change.
Insatiable means impossible to satisfy, which does not fit.

definition: not safe or secure; likely to fall or fail

examples.text: The nest sits in a precarious spot on the edge of the cliff.
The new republic's finances were precarious for its first ten years.
I carried a precarious stack of plates from the table to the sink.

confused.note: Precarious means insecure; precocious means advanced for one's age.

questions.passage: The climbers' position was ______. They stood on a ledge barely wider than their boots, with a sheer drop below and the only rope anchored to a rock that had already begun to shift.
questions.explanation: A narrow ledge and a shifting anchor make the position dangerously insecure.

distractors.why: Stagnant means not moving or developing, which does not convey danger.
Affluent means wealthy, which does not fit.
Cerebral means intellectual, which does not describe a ledge.

partsNote: from Latin precarius, "obtained by begging," so uncertain

definition: an amount that is much more than is needed

examples.text: The survey produced a plethora of data that took years to analyze.
A plethora of small kingdoms made the region impossible to govern.
The store offers a plethora of cereal brands and exactly one kind of milk.

confused.note: A plethora is too many, an excess; a myriad is simply a very large number.

questions.passage: Shoppers once had two or three toothpastes to choose from. Today they face a ______ of options, and studies suggest that so many choices leave people less satisfied with whichever tube they finally buy.
questions.explanation: So many options that they reduce satisfaction is an excess.

distractors.why: A dearth is a shortage, the opposite of too many options.
A paragon is a model of excellence, which does not fit "of options."
A zenith is a peak, which does not fit.

definition: not serious or sensible; having no useful purpose

examples.text: The court dismissed the lawsuit as frivolous.
The heroine is tired of frivolous talk about ribbons and dances.
I made the frivolous purchase of a hat for my cat.

confused.note: Frivolous means unserious or wasteful; frugal means careful with money.

questions.passage: The committee had little patience for ______ complaints. It set aside a letter objecting to the color of the town's new benches and turned its attention to reports of a collapsing bridge.
questions.explanation: A complaint about bench colors is unserious compared with a collapsing bridge.

distractors.why: Imperative means urgent and essential, the opposite of a trivial complaint.
Precarious means insecure, which describes the bridge, not the complaints set aside.
Pious means devout, which does not fit.

definition: to make someone less angry by giving them what they demand

examples.text: The king tried to appease the nobles by returning their lands.
Nothing the servants offer can appease the furious countess.
I appeased my hungry little brother with half of my sandwich.

confused.note: Appease means to calm by giving in; appraise means to judge the value of something.

questions.passage: When customers discovered that the software update had erased their saved files, they were furious. The company attempted to ______ them by offering a year of free service, though many said it was not enough.
questions.explanation: Offering free service is an attempt to calm angry customers.

distractors.why: Agitate means to stir up, the opposite of the company's aim.
Sanction means to approve or to penalize, neither of which fits.
Appraise means to assess value; it only looks like the right word.

definition: not direct or straightforward; slanting

examples.text: The letter makes only an oblique reference to the quarrel.
The low winter sun strikes the ground at an oblique angle.
Her oblique hint about "someone's birthday" was aimed at me.

confused.note: Oblique means indirect; obscure means unclear or little known.

questions.passage: The minister never criticized the president by name. Her disapproval took a more ______ form: in speeches she would praise "leaders who listen" and pause just long enough for the audience to understand.
questions.explanation: Criticism delivered through hints is indirect.

distractors.why: Strenuous means requiring great effort, which is not the contrast with naming him.
Insatiable means impossible to satisfy, which does not fit.
Archaic means old-fashioned, which does not fit.

definition: the highest or most successful point

examples.text: The empire reached its zenith under her rule and declined soon after.
At noon the sun is near its zenith, directly overhead.
The party hit its zenith when the cake arrived.

confused.note: Zenith is the highest point; nadir is the lowest.

questions.passage: The city's influence was at its ______ around the year 1500, when its ships dominated every trade route in the region. Within a century, rival ports had taken most of that trade away.
questions.explanation: Dominating every trade route marks the highest point of its influence.

distractors.why: Nadir means the lowest point, the opposite of dominance.
An epitome is a perfect example, not a high point in time.
A proclivity is a tendency, which does not fit.

definition: a person or thing that is a perfect example of a good quality

examples.text: The knight is presented as a paragon of loyalty.
The ancient republic was held up as a paragon of civic virtue.
My sister, who has never missed a deadline, is a paragon of organization.

confused.note: A paragon is a model of excellence; a parody is a mocking imitation.

questions.passage: The retiring judge was remembered as a ______ of fairness. In forty years on the bench, lawyers on both sides agreed, she had never once let her personal opinions decide a case.
questions.explanation: Never letting opinions decide a case makes her a model of fairness.

distractors.why: A plethora is an excess, which does not describe a person.
A proclivity is a tendency, which does not fit "a ______ of fairness."
A zenith is a highest point, not a person who models a virtue.

definition: a confusing and difficult problem or question

examples.text: How birds navigate across oceans remained a conundrum for centuries.
The new republic faced a conundrum: it needed taxes but had promised to abolish them.
The seating chart for the wedding was a conundrum involving three feuding uncles.

confused.note: A conundrum is a puzzling problem; a quandary is a state of uncertainty about what to do.

questions.passage: City planners face a ______. Building more roads attracts more cars and worsens traffic, yet refusing to build them leaves growing suburbs with no way to reach the center.
questions.explanation: A problem in which either choice causes trouble is confusing and difficult.

distractors.why: Serendipity is a lucky accident, which does not describe a hard problem.
A paragon is a model of excellence, which does not fit.
A bane is a cause of misery; the passage presents a puzzle about choices, not a single source of harm.

definition: caring about the needs and happiness of others more than your own

examples.text: Vampire bats show altruistic behavior, sharing food with hungry neighbors.
Her motives were altruistic: she gave away the patent so that anyone could make the vaccine.
It was altruistic of him to give up his seat on the last bus.

confused.note: Altruistic means selfless; it is unrelated to autism.

questions.passage: Skeptics assumed that the billionaire's donation was a way to reduce her taxes. In fact her motives appear to have been ______: she gave anonymously, claimed no deduction, and asked that no building be named for her.
questions.explanation: Giving anonymously with no benefit to herself is selfless.

distractors.why: Utilitarian means practical in purpose; the contrast is between selfish and selfless motives.
Specious means misleadingly attractive, which does not describe her motives.
Irascible means easily angered, which is unrelated.

definition: expressed clearly in a few words

examples.text: The abstract gives a succinct summary of the paper's findings.
The general's succinct report read, "We came, we saw, we won."
Keep the voicemail succinct: name, number, reason for calling.

confused.note: Succinct means brief and clear; distinct means separate or clearly different.

questions.passage: The first draft of the mission statement ran to three pages. The final version is admirably ______: a single sentence of nineteen words that every employee can recite from memory.
questions.explanation: One sentence in place of three pages is clear and brief.

distractors.why: Verbose means wordy, which describes the first draft.
Specious means seeming right but actually wrong, which is not the point.
Staid means serious and dull, which is not what is being praised.

partsNote: from Latin cingere, "to gird": tucked up

definition: willing to accept a suggestion or to be influenced

examples.text: The young king proved amenable to his ministers' advice.
The infection is amenable to treatment if caught early.
My parents were surprisingly amenable to the idea of a later curfew.

confused.note: Amenable means willing to go along; amiable means friendly.

questions.passage: The landlord had refused every earlier request. Tenants were therefore surprised to find her ______ to their latest proposal: she agreed to repaint the hallways if they would supply the labor.
questions.explanation: Agreeing to the proposal shows she was willing to accept it.

distractors.why: Irascible means easily angered, which does not complete "to their latest proposal."
Despondent means hopeless, which is not her reaction.
Zealous means fervently devoted, too strong for someone who merely agreed.

definition: showing skills or abilities at a much younger age than usual

examples.text: Mozart was a precocious child who composed his first symphony at eight.
The precocious narrator, age nine, corrects her tutor's Latin.
My precocious niece read the entire dinosaur encyclopedia before kindergarten.

confused.note: Precocious means advanced for one's age; precarious means insecure.

questions.passage: The mathematician was famously ______. At five she was solving problems meant for teenagers, and at twelve she published a proof that had eluded professors for decades.
questions.explanation: Solving advanced problems at five shows ability far ahead of her age.

distractors.why: Staid means sedate and unadventurous, which is not what the examples show.
Despondent means hopeless, which does not fit.
Tractable means easily managed, which is not the quality described.

partsNote: from Latin coquere, "to cook, to ripen": ripened early

definition: to become gradually weaker, smaller, or less important

examples.text: The moon waxes for two weeks and then wanes for two.
The dynasty's power waned as provincial governors grew bolder.
My enthusiasm for the puzzle waned somewhere around the thousandth piece of sky.

confused.note: To wane is to decline; to wean is to gradually stop depending on something.

questions.passage: Interest in the comet was intense during the first week, when it was visible to the naked eye. As it dimmed and drifted lower on the horizon, public enthusiasm began to ______, and the observatory's evening crowds thinned.
questions.explanation: Thinning crowds show enthusiasm gradually decreasing.

distractors.why: Burgeon means to grow rapidly, the opposite of thinning crowds.
Abscond means to run away secretly, which does not fit enthusiasm.
Obfuscate means to make unclear, which does not fit.

definition: the luck of finding good things by accident

examples.text: Serendipity played a part in the discovery of X-rays.
By pure serendipity, the heroine opens the one drawer that holds the missing letter.
It was serendipity that I found a twenty-dollar bill in my old coat on the day I forgot my wallet.

confused.note: Serendipity is a lucky accidental discovery; synchronicity is a meaningful coincidence in timing.

questions.passage: The invention owed more to ______ than to planning. A chemist trying to make a stronger glue produced a weak one instead, and it was years before a colleague realized that such a glue was perfect for removable notes.
questions.explanation: A failed experiment that turned out useful by accident is a lucky discovery.

distractors.why: Trepidation means fear, which does not explain the invention.
Equanimity means calmness, which is not what produced the glue.
A conundrum is a puzzle; the passage stresses luck over planning.

partsNote: coined from Serendip, an old name for Sri Lanka, in a tale of lucky princes

definition: a feeling of fear or worry about what is going to happen

examples.text: With some trepidation, the boy knocks on the door of the house everyone avoids.
Settlers viewed the approaching winter with trepidation.
I opened my grade report with trepidation and then exhaled.

confused.note: Trepidation is fear; intrepid means without fear.

questions.passage: The apprentice had never before been trusted with the kiln. It was with considerable ______ that she lifted the lid the next morning, half expecting to find a year's worth of pottery cracked beyond repair.
questions.explanation: Expecting disaster as she lifts the lid shows fear and worry.

distractors.why: Equanimity means calmness, the opposite of her nervous state.
Serendipity is lucky chance, which is not a feeling one acts "with."
Alacrity means cheerful eagerness, which someone expecting disaster would not feel.

definition: very sad and without hope

examples.text: Despondent after the shipwreck, the sailor stops counting the days.
The despondent army had not been paid or fed in a month.
I was despondent about my driving test until I learned I could retake it Friday.

confused.note: Despondent means hopeless; dependent means relying on someone else.

questions.passage: After the third rejection in a week, the young playwright grew ______. She stopped writing, told friends she had no talent, and spoke of giving up the theater for good.
questions.explanation: Giving up and doubting her talent show sadness and loss of hope.

distractors.why: Ebullient means overflowing with enthusiasm, the opposite of her mood.
Zealous means eagerly devoted, but she stopped writing.
Amenable means willing to go along, which does not describe despair.

partsNote: from Latin spondere, "to promise": having given up the promise of hope

definition: to officially declare that someone is not to blame for something

examples.text: New evidence exonerated the officer forty years after his conviction.
The tests exonerated the factory; the pollution came from farther upstream.
The cat was exonerated when we found the missing sock behind the dryer.

confused.note: Exonerate means to clear of blame; exaggerate means to overstate.

questions.passage: The driver had spent two years under suspicion. He was finally ______ when engineers showed that the crash had been caused by a faulty signal, not by anything he had done.
questions.explanation: Proof that the signal was at fault cleared him of blame.

distractors.why: Implicated means shown to be involved, the opposite of being cleared.
Cajoled means coaxed with flattery, which does not fit.
Obfuscated means made unclear, which does not apply to a person being cleared.

partsNote: from Latin onus, "burden": to lift the burden from

definition: a state of not being able to decide what to do

examples.text: The hero is in a quandary: betray his friend or break his oath.
The offer of peace put the council in a quandary.
Two parties on the same night left me in a quandary.

confused.note: A quandary is a state of indecision; a quarry is a place where stone is dug, or prey that is hunted.

questions.passage: The scholarship offer left Mateo in a ______. Accepting it meant moving two thousand miles from his family, but declining it meant giving up the only way he could afford to study.
questions.explanation: Two choices, each with a serious cost, leave him unable to decide.

distractors.why: Serendipity is a happy accident, not a state of indecision.
A bane is a source of harm, which does not fit "in a."
A sycophant is a flatterer, which does not fit.

definition: serious, steady, and rather dull or old-fashioned

examples.text: The staid banker surprises everyone by eloping with a trapeze artist.
The staid old newspaper refused to print photographs until 1940.
My staid uncle wears the same gray suit to every occasion, including the beach.

confused.note: Staid means sedate; stayed is the past tense of stay.

questions.passage: The firm had a reputation for being ______. Its lawyers wore dark suits, its offices had not been redecorated since 1950, and its annual party consisted of tea and a speech.
questions.explanation: Dark suits, old offices, and a tea party suggest a sober, unadventurous firm.

distractors.why: Ebullient means bubbling with enthusiasm, the opposite of this firm.
Precocious means advanced for one's age, which does not fit.
Specious means misleadingly plausible, which does not describe a firm's style.

definition: seeming true or right at first but actually false

examples.text: The ad makes the specious claim that "natural" always means safe.
The invasion was justified by a specious argument about protecting trade.
"Everyone else is doing it" is a specious reason, as my mother likes to say.

confused.note: Specious means sounding right but wrong; spurious means fake or not genuine.

questions.passage: The salesman's reasoning was ______. He argued that because the more expensive model had more buttons it must do more, an appealing idea until one learned that half the buttons performed the same function.
questions.explanation: Reasoning that sounds appealing but proves false is specious.

distractors.why: Succinct means brief and clear, which is not the flaw described.
Salient means most noticeable, which does not describe faulty reasoning.
Altruistic means selfless, which a sales pitch is not.

definition: calmness of mind, especially in a difficult situation

examples.text: The queen received news of the defeat with equanimity and asked for a map.
Nothing disturbs the gardener's equanimity, not even hail in June.
My mom handled the flat tire with equanimity; I handled it with panic.

confused.note: Equanimity is calmness of mind; equality is the state of being equal.

questions.passage: Passengers on the delayed flight grumbled and paced, but the elderly woman in seat 4A accepted the news with ______. She took out her knitting and remarked that an airport was as good a place to sit as any.
questions.explanation: Calmly knitting while others grumble shows composure.

distractors.why: Trepidation means fear or worry, which she did not show.
Serendipity is lucky chance, which does not describe a reaction.
Rancor means bitter resentment, the opposite of her calm acceptance.

definition: easily made angry

examples.text: The irascible colonel shouts at the weather, the mail, and his soup.
The irascible admiral dismissed three captains in a single afternoon.
My irascible neighbor yells whenever a ball lands in his yard.

confused.note: Irascible means quick to anger; erasable means able to be erased.

questions.passage: Staff learned to approach the ______ editor with care. A misplaced comma could provoke a shouted lecture, and he once threw a dictionary across the newsroom over a misspelled headline.
questions.explanation: Shouting over commas and throwing a dictionary show he is easily angered.

distractors.why: Amenable means agreeable and cooperative, which he was not.
Staid means sedate and calm, which does not describe someone who throws books.
Altruistic means selfless, which is unrelated.

definition: to make something unclear or hard to understand, often on purpose

examples.text: The minister's long answer was meant to obfuscate, not to explain.
Jargon can obfuscate a simple finding.
The fine print seems designed to obfuscate how much the phone really costs.

confused.note: To obfuscate is to make unclear; to obviate is to make unnecessary.

questions.passage: Critics accused the company of trying to ______ the true cost of its loans. The interest rate appeared on page one in large type, while the fees that doubled the total were scattered through forty pages of small print.
questions.explanation: Burying fees in small print makes the true cost hard to see.

distractors.why: Elucidate means to make clear, the opposite of hiding fees.
Exonerate means to clear of blame, which does not fit "the true cost."
Cajole means to coax, which does not fit.

definition: easy to manage, control, or deal with

examples.text: Splitting the question into parts made the problem more tractable.
The governor found the merchants more tractable once the port reopened.
A tired toddler is rarely a tractable one.

confused.note: Tractable means manageable; trackable means able to be followed.

questions.passage: The original equation was too complex for any computer of the day to solve. By assuming that the particles were perfect spheres, the physicists turned it into a far more ______ problem.
questions.explanation: A simplifying assumption made the problem easier to manage.

distractors.why: Intractable means very hard to deal with, which describes the original equation.
Salient means prominent, which does not describe an easier problem.
Utilitarian means designed for practical use, which is not the point.

partsNote: able to be pulled or led

definition: a person who flatters powerful people to gain advantage

examples.text: The court was full of sycophants who told the emperor only what he wished to hear.
The duke prefers one honest enemy to a dozen sycophants.
Nobody likes a sycophant who laughs too hard at the boss's jokes.

confused.note: A sycophant is a flatterer; the words only sound alike.

questions.passage: The chief executive complained that she was surrounded by ______. Whatever she proposed, her deputies called brilliant, and she could not remember the last time one of them had told her she was wrong.
questions.explanation: Deputies who praise everything and never disagree are flatterers.

distractors.why: Iconoclasts attack accepted ideas, the opposite of deputies who always agree.
Paragons are models of excellence, which she would not complain about.
Conundrums are puzzles, not people.

definition: to persuade someone to do something by gentle urging or flattery

examples.text: The fox cajoles the crow into singing and dropping the cheese.
The envoy cajoled the reluctant chiefs into attending the council.
I cajoled my brother into driving me by promising to wash his car.

confused.note: To cajole is to persuade with charm; to coerce is to force with threats.

questions.passage: The toddler refused to put on her shoes, and scolding only made her cry. Her grandfather tried a different approach: with jokes, praise, and the promise of a story, he ______ her into them in under a minute.
questions.explanation: Jokes, praise, and promises are gentle persuasion.

distractors.why: Coerced means forced by threats, far too harsh for jokes and praise.
Exonerated means cleared of blame, which does not fit.
Obfuscated means made unclear, which does not fit.

definition: full of cheerful energy and excitement

examples.text: The ebullient cousin bursts in with armfuls of presents and news.
The ebullient crowd carried the winning candidate through the streets.
My ebullient lab partner cheers every time a reaction changes color.

confused.note: Ebullient means bubbling with enthusiasm; an emollient softens or soothes.

questions.passage: The team's coach is as ______ as its manager is reserved. While the manager watches silently from the bench, the coach bounds along the sideline, laughing, clapping, and shouting encouragement.
questions.explanation: Bounding, laughing, and shouting encouragement show lively enthusiasm.

distractors.why: Staid means sedate, which better describes the manager.
Irascible means easily angered; the coach is cheerful, not bad-tempered.
Despondent means hopeless, the opposite of his energy.

partsNote: from Latin bullire, "to boil": boiling over

definition: to leave secretly and quickly, often to avoid being caught

examples.text: The treasurer absconded with the city's gold on the eve of the audit.
The clerk absconds to the coast with his employer's cash box.
The dog absconded with an entire roast chicken while we were saying grace.

confused.note: To abscond is to run off secretly; to abstain is to refrain.

questions.passage: Investors arrived at the firm's offices to find the doors locked and the desks cleared. The founder, it emerged, had ______ during the night, taking with him the contents of the company's accounts.
questions.explanation: Leaving secretly at night with the money is running off to avoid capture.

distractors.why: Waned means gradually declined, which does not describe a sudden flight.
Cajoled means coaxed, which does not fit.
Exonerated means cleared of blame, which he certainly was not.

definition: something that causes great trouble or unhappiness

examples.text: Pirates were the bane of merchants on that coast for a century.
Rust is the bane of iron bridges.
Group texts that buzz all night are the bane of my existence.

confused.note: A bane is a source of harm; a boon is a benefit. They are opposites.

questions.passage: For farmers along the river, the spring floods were once a ______, sweeping away fences and drowning seedlings. Since the new levee was built, the same floods have been channeled into ponds that water the fields all summer.
questions.explanation: Floods that destroyed fences and seedlings were a source of great trouble.

distractors.why: A boon is a benefit, which is what the floods became only after the levee.
A quandary is a state of indecision, which does not describe destructive floods.
A paragon is a model of excellence, which does not fit.

definition: most noticeable or important

examples.text: The report's most salient finding is that sea levels are rising faster than predicted.
The salient feature of the new constitution was its limit on royal power.
The salient point of Mom's speech was "be home by ten."

confused.note: Salient means prominent; saline means salty.

questions.passage: The committee's report runs to four hundred pages, but its ______ points can be stated in a sentence: the dam is safe for now, will need repairs within ten years, and should not be made any taller.
questions.explanation: The points that matter most are the most important ones.

distractors.why: Specious means falsely plausible, which is not how the report's main points are presented.
Tractable means manageable, which does not describe points in a report.
Staid means sedate, which does not fit.

partsNote: from Latin salire, "to leap": leaping out

definition: designed to be useful, not attractive or comfortable

examples.text: The army's utilitarian huts had no windows and a single stove.
She trades her silk gowns for utilitarian gray wool.
My backpack is utilitarian: ugly, enormous, and impossible to break.

confused.note: Utilitarian means practical; utopian means idealistic and perfect in theory.

questions.passage: The architect's early buildings were strictly ______. Their concrete walls, exposed pipes, and plain steel doors served their purposes well, but nobody ever called them beautiful.
questions.explanation: Buildings that work well but are not beautiful are designed for use.

distractors.why: Ornate means richly decorated, the opposite of plain concrete and steel.
Ebullient means cheerfully energetic, which does not describe buildings.
Salient means prominent, which is not the contrast with "beautiful."

definition: showing great energy and enthusiasm for a cause or goal

examples.text: Zealous reformers closed every theater in the city.
The zealous young researcher slept in the lab during the final week of the trial.
The zealous hall monitor wrote up a teacher for running.

confused.note: Zealous means eagerly devoted; jealous means envious.

questions.passage: The new inspector was more ______ than her predecessor, who had visited each restaurant once a year. She arrived unannounced every month, checked every refrigerator, and stayed until the last pot was washed.
questions.explanation: Monthly surprise visits and thorough checks show energetic devotion to the job.

distractors.why: Despondent means hopeless, which does not fit her energy.
Amenable means easily persuaded, which is not the comparison being made.
Jealous means envious; it only sounds like the right word.
